title: N-Queens
oneLinerQuestion: Place n queens on an n x n chessboard so that no two queens attack each other.
explanation:
Problem Intuition: The N-Queens puzzle requires placing N non-attacking queens on an N x N chessboard such that no two queens share the same row, column, or diagonal. Placing queens row by row inherently satisfies the row constraint (exactly one queen per row). To evaluate whether a column or diagonal is already under attack in O(1) time without rescanning the board, we track occupied vertical lines and both diagonal orientations using HashSets during recursive Backtracking (Depth-First Search).

- Step 1: Constraint Tracking via Diagonal Invariants — Any cell at coordinate (r, c) belongs to two diagonals. Along positive diagonals (sloping upward/right), the sum (r + c) remains constant. Along negative diagonals (sloping downward/right), the difference (r - c) remains constant. We maintain three Sets: 'cols' to track occupied columns, 'posDiag' for (r + c), and 'negDiag' for (r - c).

- Step 2: Recursive Backtracking Signature — We define a helper function backtrack(row, board) starting at row 0. The current board state can be represented as an array of row configurations or placed column indices.

- Step 3: Base Case & Solution Recording — When row === N, we have safely placed N non-attacking queens across all N rows. We construct the string board representation (placing 'Q' at designated column coordinates and '.' elsewhere), append this snapshot to our results list, and return.

- Step 4: Iterative Column Selection & Conflict Checking — For the current row, we loop through every column 'col' from 0 to N - 1. We test if placing a queen at (row, col) is safe: cols.has(col) || posDiag.has(row + col) || negDiag.has(row - col). If any of these sets contain the value, the square is threatened, and we skip to the next column.

- Step 5: Placement, Recursion, & State Restoration — If the position is safe, we record the placement by adding 'col' to 'cols', 'row + col' to 'posDiag', and 'row - col' to 'negDiag'. We then proceed to the next row with backtrack(row + 1, board). Upon return, we backtrack by removing those coordinates from all three Sets, cleanly restoring state for the next candidate column.

- Complexity & Memory Guarantees — Time Complexity: O(N!) because placing a queen in each successive row reduces the available valid column choices. Space Complexity: O(N) auxiliary space to maintain the recursion call stack and the three lookup sets.
pseudoCode:
FUNCTION solveNQueens(n):
    res = [], cols = SET(), posDiag = SET(), negDiag = SET(), board = MATRIX(n, n, '.')
    FUNCTION backtrack(r):
        IF r == n THEN APPEND FORMAT(board) TO res; RETURN
        FOR c FROM 0 TO n - 1 DO:
            IF c IN cols OR (r+c) IN posDiag OR (r-c) IN negDiag THEN CONTINUE
            ADD c TO cols, ADD r+c TO posDiag, ADD r-c TO negDiag
            board[r][c] = 'Q'
            backtrack(r + 1)
            REMOVE c FROM cols, REMOVE r+c FROM posDiag, REMOVE r-c FROM negDiag
            board[r][c] = '.'
        END FOR
    END FUNCTION
    backtrack(0)
    RETURN res
END FUNCTION
